A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. A 42-year-old man with 30 pack-years of smoking, cannabis use, alcohol dependence, and the use of herbal products for addiction cessation presented with a 3-day history of acute urinary retention, hematemesis, and progressive neurological deficits. On day 3, he developed marked paraparesis of the lower limbs (muscle strength 2/5), was unable to stand or walk, and had hyperreflexia with sustained clonus in the lower extremities. Sensory function—including proprioception, light touch, and vibration—was normal. He also had hypertonic sphincters and hyperalgesia. Cranial nerve and upper limb examinations were normal. He was febrile, and his condition deteriorated into respiratory distress requiring intubation and sedation.

Lumbar puncture revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid without albuminocytologic dissociation: glucose 0.49 g/L, protein 0.20 g/L, chloride 121 mmol/L, 14 white blood cells (70% lymphocytes), and 14 red blood cells per mm³; cultures were sterile. Blood tests showed anemia (hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL falling to 8.2 g/dL), leukocytosis (18 350 cells/μL), platelet counts fluctuating between 98 000 and 136 000 cells/μL, hyponatremia corrected from 117.5 mEq/L to 146 mEq/L over 8 days, potassium levels between 5.5 and 4.6 mEq/L, elevated AST (134 U/L) and ALT (65.9 U/L), and CRP 128.8–131.2 mg/L. Renal function remained normal.

Initial brain MRI showed multiple bilateral, symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions in the periventricular and periaqueductal regions, dorsomedial thalami, medial temporal lobes, caudate nuclei, and brainstem, with diffusion restriction and low ADC values. Spinal MRI demonstrated diffuse T2 hyperintensities throughout the cervical, thoracic, and lumbar cord. A follow-up MRI a few days later revealed worsening of these lesions, new involvement of the lenticular nuclei, and patchy contrast enhancement in the cerebral peduncles, superior cerebellar peduncles, superior colliculi, right pons, and bilateral medulla. There was more extensive bilateral FLAIR hyperintensity in the medial temporal lobes and periventricular white matter and progression of the spinal cord lesions.

Contrast-enhanced CT showed lymphadenopathy in the bilateral cervical and axillary regions, left inguinal lymphadenopathy, and marked peri- and pararenal soft-tissue infiltration.
